title_en: A City Moves into the Night
description_ru: Выдуманная новость о городе, где из-за жары власти перевели всю жизнь на ночное время, и о том, как горожане к этому приспособились.
text:
QASRIVEH, Republic of Zeldaria. At a few minutes after nine on Monday evening, the municipal siren of Qasriveh sounded, shop shutters rattled upwards along the length of the Avenue of Tamarinds, and some four hundred thousand citizens stepped out of their houses, blinking, to begin the working day. The city, which has endured the hottest summer in its recorded history, has formally become the first in the world to adopt a fully nocturnal schedule, an experiment its mayor described as "a bold act of adaptation" and his critics as "a very elaborate way of avoiding the sun."

The decision, ratified by the city council after a record-breaking heatwave that lasted fifty-three days and melted, among other things, the tarmac outside the town hall, shifts the municipal clock by twelve hours. Offices, schools, markets and law courts now open at dusk and close at dawn, while the daylight hours, in which temperatures regularly exceed forty-eight degrees, have been designated a period of "civic repose," during which citizens are encouraged to sleep, to shelter in the cool of their cellars and to refrain from anything more strenuous than a lukewarm bath.

The mayor, Idris Valkenburg-Tanaka, announced the plan at a press conference held, with a fine sense of the symbolic, at midnight. "For centuries our ancestors lived by the rhythms of the sun," he said, standing beneath a lantern, "and, on the whole, it served them rather well. But the sun has changed its terms. We are therefore obliged to negotiate, and the first rule of negotiation is that one should be somewhere else when the other party arrives."

Adjustment has been, by all accounts, turbulent. On the first night, the city's bakers, accustomed to rising before dawn, found themselves working in the middle of a crowd of customers demanding breakfast at midnight, and were reportedly baffled to discover that the traditional notion of "morning bread" had become philosophically problematic. Schoolchildren, who had at first greeted the reform as a sort of permanent party, have since developed an uneasy relationship with their homework, which they now complete in the small hours, beneath a moon that is, as one pupil complained, "a rubbish desk lamp."

The effects on commerce have been remarkable. Restaurants, formerly deserted during the oppressive afternoons, report an unprecedented boom in business, while the nightclub industry, which used to enjoy a monopoly on darkness, has been plunged into an existential crisis. "How can one stay out until dawn," lamented one proprietor, "when the whole city is out until dawn? It is like being the only man in the pub who is sober, except that everyone else is also sober, and awake, and discussing the tax return." He has since converted his premises into a tax advisory.

Less welcome, to some, has been the revival of nocturnal habits long thought obsolete. The city's bats, who had previously considered the hours after sunset to be their private domain, have lodged what the zoological society has described as "a vigorous, if silent, protest," and residents report that the cooperation of owls has been grudging at best. A local ornithologist remarked that he had never before witnessed a creature of the night look so profoundly annoyed to be asked for directions.

Practical difficulties abound, and are being addressed with the unflappable resourcefulness of a population that has recently learnt to be flexible about breakfast. Street lighting, designed for an occasional pedestrian, is being augmented at considerable expense; the postal service has had to explain that the term "first post" no longer has any meaning; and the city's solitary astronomer, Professor Ottoline Brandvold-Achebe, has voiced a certain unease at the sudden competition for the best vantage points on the roof of the observatory. "I have waited forty years for the dark," she said, "and now it is full of people asking me what the little lights are."

Not all citizens are convinced, naturally, and some are openly mutinous. A protest group calling itself the Daylight Defenders, whose members assemble at noon beneath a vast parasol in the central square, argues that the scheme is an admission of defeat, and that the correct response to a hostile climate is to improve the air conditioning. Their spokesman, a pale gentleman named Lazlo Merriweather-Kaya, who said that he had not been outdoors before sunset in a fortnight, acknowledged that the demonstration was poorly attended. "It is the heat," he explained, with the dignity of a man defending a lost cause beneath a large umbrella.

Public health officials, meanwhile, report encouraging signs. Heatstroke admissions have fallen by almost ninety per cent, electricity consumption has dropped in the afternoon peak, and the cost of fruit has declined, owing to the fact that the orchards are now harvested at night by workers who are paid to eat a certain amount of it. Doctors have noted a modest increase in the number of patients complaining about insomnia, though the majority appear to be those who are merely sleeping at the wrong hour and are waking up angry in the middle of the afternoon.

There are, naturally, social consequences that no planner foresaw. The city's romantic traditions, which depend heavily upon sunsets, have required a hasty adjustment; couples now exchange vows at dawn, a ceremony that proves, in practice, to be a rather melancholy affair, since the guests are exhausted and the groom, as a rule, is yawning. Meanwhile, the tourist board has begun to market the city as "the capital of the late riser," and has recorded an inundation of enquiries from other cities, several of which have sent delegations to observe the experiment, wearing sunglasses and some apprehension.

At four o'clock on Tuesday morning, as the mayor strolled through the market, surveying the stalls by lamplight, an elderly fruit seller pressed a melon into his hands. "It is cooler," she said, "and we sell more. In forty years, I have never been so pleased to see the moon." The mayor, according to an aide, was visibly moved. The melon, he said afterwards, was excellent, and he intends to eat it at some point during the afternoon, when he is fully asleep.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Язык не касается нёба, губы слегка округлены; английское r мягкое, не раскатистое.
Губы вытянуты вперёд, без касания зубов; не произносите как русское «в».
Кончик языка между зубами, голос включён; не заменяйте на «з» или «д».
В длинных словах одно ударение; последующие слоги заметно слабее, гласные в них сводятся к ə.

questions.question: Why did Qasriveh move its schedule to nighttime?
questions.answer: Because of extreme heat in the summer.

questions.question: What do shops and offices do during the day?
questions.answer: They close for civic repose, so citizens sleep.

questions.question: What happened to heatstroke cases?
questions.answer: They fell by almost ninety per cent.
